big: Meena has a credit card dues of ₹50,000, a personal loan and a home loan. She sends a bit to each every month and still the total barely moves. The order of payment matters.

lines: I have three loans. Where should my spare ₹5,000 go?
To the one that costs the most per month, after you have paid the minimum on all. Let us compare what each costs.

alt: Two bars comparing one month of interest on a card and on a home loan
caps: ₹50,000 owed on a card (3% a month) costs ₹1,500 in a single month.
The same ₹50,000 on a home loan at 8.5% a year costs about ₹354 a month.
These are assumed rates. The gap is the point: the card costs over four times as much.
Pay the costliest debt first, after minimums on all.

intro: For most households, this order works.
rows: Never miss a minimum payment or EMI
Pay off the costliest debt, usually cards
Then build the full emergency fund
Invest alongside cheaper loans like a home loan
note: Missed payments damage your credit score, so minimums always come first.

q: A card charges 3% a month. Rohan pays only the minimum amount due each month. What happens?
opts: The debt clears quickly, since the bank wants it settled on time
Most of the balance stays and keeps attracting interest at a high rate
The interest stops once he pays the minimum for three months
The balance is cut each month by the amount of interest charged
why: The minimum is a small slice of the bill, so the debt can linger for a very long time.
The minimum covers little of the balance, so the rest keeps growing at the card's high rate.
Interest keeps running on the unpaid part. Paying the minimum does not stop it.
Interest is added to the balance. The minimum rarely cuts it by much.

q: Meena has a card at 3% a month and a home loan at 8.5% a year. She has ₹5,000 spare above all minimums. Where does it go?
opts: To the home loan, since it is the larger debt overall in rupees
Split equally between the two, so neither of them feels ignored
Into shares, since returns will certainly beat both of the loan rates
To the card, since it costs far more each month than the home loan does
why: Size does not decide it. The cost of each rupee of debt does, and the card costs more.
Splitting leaves the costly card running longer than it should.
Share returns are uncertain, while the card's interest is certain and very high.
The card's rate is many times higher, so paying it first saves the most interest.

q: What is the avalanche method of repaying several debts?
opts: Pay minimums on all, then put spare money on the highest-rate debt
Pay the smallest balance first, to get some quick wins early on
Pay every debt an equal amount, regardless of the interest rate it carries
Pay the oldest debt first, since it has been running the longest
why: The avalanche targets the highest rate first, which saves the most total interest.
That is the snowball method. It is motivating, but not the cheapest.
Equal payments ignore which debt is most costly, so more interest is paid in all.
Age does not decide the cost. The interest rate does.

q: Rohan has a home loan at a moderate rate and also ₹20,000 spare each month. What is a sensible plan?
opts: Put every rupee into the loan, since all debt must be cleared as fast as it can be
Stop paying the EMI, since the spare money is enough to cover it for her
Let the home loan run, and invest alongside once costlier debts are cleared
Take a new loan to invest, since returns are always higher than loan rates
why: Not all debt needs to be rushed. A moderate-rate loan can run while other goals progress.
Missing EMIs harms the credit score and adds charges, so the EMI must be paid on time.
A moderate-rate home loan can run while he invests, once costlier debt is cleared.
Borrowing to invest adds risk. Returns are uncertain while the loan cost is certain.

pts: Pay minimums on every debt first, so nothing goes overdue.
Then send spare money to the costliest debt, usually a card.
A moderate-rate home loan can run while you also invest.
